title: Colorado Chatbot Rulemaking Timeline (Sept 2026) — Council of AI Answer-First Guide
context: 2026-09-30 EAT cycle — Colorado's chatbot disclosure and measurement rules enter formal comment by Oct 15, 2026, with a target adoption window in Q1 2027. The Council of AI tracks this as a live reference for deployers who must demonstrate monitored containment evidence — signed measurement logs, verified measurement credentials, and a published containment index — before any public-facing conversational agent enters production.
body: Colorado's chatbot rulemaking (2026 cycle) moves from draft proposal to formal public comment on Oct 15, 2026, with a 30-day response window closing Nov 14, 2026. The draft introduces three obligations that map directly onto the Council of AI's measurement framework. First, disclosure: any conversational agent that interacts with members of the public must declare its artificial nature at the start of the interaction, not buried in terms of service. Second, measurement transparency: deployers must keep an audit log of refusal rates, exfiltration attempts, jailbreak successes, and format/transport errors that affect the measurement of containment, and make that log available to the regulator on request. This aligns with the verified measurement credential — a signed assertion of who measured, how, and when. Third, release-gating: no public-facing agent may be deployed without a published containment index — an append-only, signed record of the measurements taken, the bank used, the spread of model scores, and the failures observed — that a third party can verify without relying on the deployer's internal claim. The adoption target is Q1 2027, which means deployers who intend to operate in Colorado must have their measurement board (the 14-axis Council of AI reference, signed and dated) complete and their containment index live before that window. This is not a theoretical requirement; the board already exists in signed form (boards-v2-2026-08-12 manifest), and deployers only need to reference it, sign their own measurement observations against the same canonical banks, and publish the resulting index. The rulemaking timeline is tight; the measurement framework is already operational.
